title: Nuh Raids Seize 7,600 kg of Suspected Synthetic Paneer Headed for Delhi-NCR
excerpt: Overnight raids on four unlicensed units in Haryana's Nuh district recovered tonnes of suspected analogue paneer and the chemicals used to make it, in a crackdown aimed at the Delhi-NCR wholesale food chain.
body:
• Nearly 7,600 kg of suspected synthetic paneer was seized in overnight raids on September 10-11 at four illegal manufacturing units in Nuh, Haryana — three along the Gurgaon canal in Gondola village and one in Nai.
  • Officials also recovered milk powder, refined palm oil, soybean, fabric whitener, industrial-grade bleaching agents and white poster colour — materials allegedly used to manufacture analogue paneer.
  • The product was intended for wholesale markets, catering kitchens, banquet halls and restaurants across Delhi-NCR, including Delhi, Gurugram, Faridabad, Noida and Mathura.
  • Lab results are still pending, but one check applies right now: genuine packaged paneer lists only milk and acidulants on its label. Products built on vegetable fats or starches are classified as analogues — buy from branded or licensed dairy sources when in India.

A joint enforcement team worked through the night of September 10 to 5 am on September 11, raiding four unlicensed paneer-making units in Haryana’s Nuh district and seizing nearly 7,600 kg of suspected synthetic paneer. The operation brought together the Punahana sub-divisional magistrate, the duty magistrate, the deputy superintendent of police, the Haryana State Pollution Control Board and the district Food and Drug Administration. Four product samples were sent for laboratory analysis; the rest of the seized material was destroyed on the spot under a formal panchnama.

The raids hit Yusuf Dairy, Khalid-Israel Dairy, Pandit Dairy and Saddam Dairy, with teams led by Food Safety Officer Vikas Jaglan, SDM Amit Kumar, Sadar SHO Naresh Kumar and Tehsildar Sanjeev Nagar, according to News18. Nuh Superintendent of Police Arpit Jain said an investigation had begun and an FIR would follow.

“Our teams are coordinating with the administrative authorities and we will register an FIR against the culprits and take further appropriate legal action.”

— Arpit Jain, Superintendent of Police, Nuh

A crackdown on analogue paneer

The raids are part of a widening enforcement drive against non-dairy or “analogue” paneer in Haryana. The state has prohibited the manufacture and sale of analogue paneer, and the Food Safety Commissioner has invoked Section 30(2)(a) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, banning preparation of such products with milk powder or vegetable oil. About a month earlier, the government had ordered a one-year ban on paneer production in Nuh itself — yet officials say more than three dozen illegal units still operate in the district, and the clandestine network extends to Katpuri, Bara Bazidpur, Raniyala, Bodi Kothi and Sheikhpur.

How the fake is made

The economics explain the scale. Genuine paneer needs roughly five to six litres of whole milk per kilogram, tying costs to farmgate milk prices. Operators allegedly reconstituted cheap milk solids with non-dairy hydrogenated fats and chemical stabilizers, undercutting organized dairy processors by more than half the prevailing market price, according to eDairy News India. At the four units, inspectors found low-grade vegetable oils, industrial starches, chemical emulsifiers, detergent residue, fabric whitener and white poster colour — alongside substandard conditions with no food hygiene compliance and no statutory licenses.

Why Delhi-NCR’s supply chain is the concern

Authorities suspect the finished product — reportedly stacked for morning dispatch — was bound for bulk wholesale markets across the National Capital Region. Officials say paneer made at some Punhana-area dairies reaches Delhi, Faridabad, Gurugram, Noida and Mathura, where it passes into catering kitchens, banquet facilities and restaurants and can end up served in tikkas, patties and curries. On September 26 and 27, police intercepted another 600 kg of “inedible” paneer in trucks heading to Gurugram, which the food safety department declared unfit for human consumption and buried.

What this means for the diaspora

For diaspora readers visiting Delhi-NCR, the practical exposure sits at the cheapest end of the supply chain: wedding catering, banquet halls, street-food stalls and budget restaurant thalis where paneer is bought in bulk on price. The quickest check is the label — FSSAI’s position is that authentic paneer lists only milk and acidulants, while products built on vegetable fats or starches count as analogues. States including Maharashtra, Karnataka and Gujarat already impose local restrictions. Paneer on regulated shelves abroad is a different matter; this is a supply-chain enforcement problem in India’s informal wholesale channels, not a brand problem.

What’s next

The laboratory reports on the four samples will be the trigger for prosecutions, establishing composition and anchoring charges under the Food Safety and Standards Act. Nuh Deputy Commissioner Akhil Pilani has signaled continued enforcement, calling it a zero-tolerance approach, with food-safety and pollution-control teams set to keep inspecting suspected manufacturing locations across the district. FSSAI’s draft national labeling rules could give inspectors a uniform framework for separating genuine paneer from analogues — and with the National Human Rights Commission already issuing notices in August 2026 over paneer substitutes, the pressure is for convictions, not just seizures.
image_caption: A block of paneer with cut cubes on a wooden board. The image accompanies coverage of the September 10-11 raids in Nuh, Haryana, where officials seized nearly 7,600 kg of suspected synthetic paneer.
nri_angle: Diaspora readers visiting Delhi-NCR should know cheap bulk paneer in catering and informal markets may be adulterated; genuine paneer lists only milk and acidulants, and the risk is concentrated in unregulated wholesale channels, not branded products at home or abroad.
